name: Euler characteristic
use_when: Use it when a surface has been divided into countable pieces and the question needs a whole-surface account rather than the details of one drawing. The point is not the pieces themselves; the point is whether a chosen piece account can speak for the finished carrier after the drawing is refined.
object_needed: The object is the completed surface together with a valid cell or triangulation account: vertices, edges, faces, and any boundary behavior that changes the ledger. The reader has to know what has been glued, capped, cut, or left as boundary before the count can belong to the surface instead of to the sketch.
allowed_move: The allowed move is to refine, redraw, or replace the cell division while keeping the same completed surface, the same boundary conditions, and the same gluing information. New corners, edges, or regions may appear, but they must be bookkeeping changes inside the same surface, not a quiet change of the object being counted.
protected_evidence: The protected evidence is the alternating count. Internal refinements change separate counts, but the artificial vertex-edge-face changes cancel in the final account. That cancellation is why the number can later constrain a vector-field total: it is attached to the whole carrier, not to one convenient mesh.
conclusion_it_can_force: It can identify a whole-surface constraint and later control total vector-field index. It cannot by itself describe every geometric feature of the surface, measure its bending, or tell where a defect sits. Its force is narrower and more useful: any later local account must fit this whole-surface ledger.
breaks_if: It breaks if the counted pieces do not describe the actual surface, if boundary terms are ignored, or if the count is treated as belonging to one drawing rather than to the surface. It also breaks when a gluing rule is forgotten, because then the ledger is being balanced for the wrong finished object.
everyday_test: Can the reader say what surface is being counted, what pieces make the account, and why changing the breakup leaves the final number fixed? Point to one possible refinement and explain why the extra entries cancel instead of changing the surface's account.

name: Generic position
use_when: Use it when a drawing has fragile coincidences and the proof needs clean, separate events before it can count, assign signs, or inspect defects. It is the theorem-contract version of clearing fog from the picture: the cleanup is allowed only if the original question survives the cleanup.
object_needed: The object is the same curve, surface, map, or field after a small legal nudge that removes special alignments without changing the question or the carrier space. The contract needs both halves: what was nudged, and what was kept fixed enough that the cleaned picture still answers the starting problem.
allowed_move: The allowed move is a tiny adjustment that keeps the protected relation, boundary rule, and surrounding space intact while removing accidental tangencies or multiple meetings. The move is not permission to redraw by taste; it is permission to replace a fragile accident by nearby ordinary events that the later count can inspect.
protected_evidence: The protected evidence is the stable pattern that remains after accidents are removed: clean meetings, isolated defects, or ordinary local behavior that the proof can inspect one event at a time. The important detail is that the cleanup makes evidence readable without changing the reason that evidence matters.
conclusion_it_can_force: It can make a count or sign rule honest enough to use. It does not prove that special cases are irrelevant; it prepares the ordinary case and then controls how special cases are approached. The conclusion is a prepared setting for a later argument, not the later theorem's payoff by itself.
breaks_if: It breaks if the nudge changes the object, crosses a forbidden boundary, removes a required contact, or silently changes the protected count that the later argument needs. In plain terms, it fails when the cleanup solves an easier problem and then borrows the old problem's conclusion.
everyday_test: Can the reader name the coincidence being removed, say what count or sign becomes readable afterward, and explain why the small move leaves the original question unchanged? Identify the exact protected feature before celebrating the cleaner drawing.

name: Signed intersection number
use_when: Use it when two oriented objects meet cleanly and the question is whether legal motion can remove all meetings without changing the surrounding problem. The useful question is not how many crossings the eye sees now, but whether the signed account can survive every legal redraw.
object_needed: The objects are the meeting subspaces, the surrounding space they live in, and an orientation rule that gives each clean meeting a plus or minus sign. Without the surrounding space and the sign rule, a crossing is only a visual event, not evidence that can travel through a proof.
allowed_move: The allowed move is a deformation that keeps the objects in the right surrounding space and inspects births or deaths of meeting pairs as local events. The proof has to watch what happens when two meetings are born together or disappear together, because that is where an ordinary crossing count would change.
protected_evidence: The protected evidence is the signed total. Opposite-sign pairs can appear or disappear without changing the total because their contributions cancel under the shared orientation rule. The mathematical idea is that the account ignores harmless local noise but keeps the obstruction that legal motion cannot erase.
conclusion_it_can_force: A nonzero signed total can force some meeting to remain under legal motion. It can turn a visual crossing question into durable arithmetic, but it does not locate every meeting or describe their exact shapes. It only says that the signed obstruction cannot be reduced to nothing by permitted motion.
breaks_if: It breaks if signs have no orientation source, if meetings are not clean, or if the deformation lets the objects pass through a forbidden move. It also breaks if the reader counts crossings before checking whether plus and minus signs have been earned by the geometry of the setup.
everyday_test: Can the reader explain where each sign comes from, what legal motion could create a newly born pair, and why that pair contributes no net evidence? Include why ordinary counting would be too fragile and why signed counting fixes exactly that problem.

name: Graph and diagonal fixed-point test
use_when: Use it when a rule sends inputs to outputs in the same setting and the question is whether some input is sent back to itself. This contract is useful because it replaces an invisible sentence, 'the rule returns this point,' with a visible meeting between two objects.
object_needed: The object is a rule from a space back into that same space, its graph in input-output space, and the diagonal that records equality between input and output. The same-space condition is not a technical ornament; without it, the diagonal would be comparing things that do not belong in one account.
allowed_move: The allowed move is to translate the rule into its graph without changing the domain, target, or meaning of equality between input and output. The graph is allowed to represent the rule only point by point: each graph point must still remember exactly which input produced which output.
protected_evidence: The protected evidence is the exact equivalence between graph meeting diagonal and self-agreement of the original rule, point by point in the same space. A diagonal meeting is not a metaphor; it is the statement that input and output coordinates have become the same record.
conclusion_it_can_force: It can turn a fixed-point question into an intersection question. By itself it identifies what a fixed point means; extra shape or continuity reasoning is needed to force existence. The contract explains the translation, while Brouwer-style reasoning supplies the pressure that makes a meeting unavoidable.
breaks_if: It breaks if the graph is drawn for the wrong rule, if the rule does not map the space back into itself, if the diagonal belongs to a different space, or if the domain has been changed. Any one of those mistakes makes the meeting test answer a different equality question.
everyday_test: Can the reader point to one graph point and say which input and output it records, then explain why diagonal meeting means self-agreement? Also say what further fact, such as continuity or a no-escape shape, would be needed to prove a meeting exists.

name: Brouwer fixed-point theorem
use_when: Use it when a continuous rule sends a closed filled ball back into itself and the goal is to prove that some point stays put. The theorem is about unavoidable self-agreement under a strict container rule, not about finding the point by calculation.
object_needed: The object is the closed filled ball, including its interior and boundary, plus a continuous self-map that never sends points outside the ball. The filled interior matters because a hollow shell, an open region, or a rule that escapes the region has a different set of possible evasions.
allowed_move: The allowed move is to use continuity and the filled shape's boundary constraint to rule out a total escape from self-agreement for every point at once. In everyday terms, the rule may push points around, but it is not allowed to jump or push the whole ball outside itself.
protected_evidence: The protected evidence is the no-escape structure of a closed filled ball under a continuous self-map that stays inside the same ball. The boundary and the no-jump condition work together: every proposed escape plan has to remain coherent across neighboring points and across the edge.
conclusion_it_can_force: It can force existence of at least one fixed point. It does not compute the point, say it is unique, or describe the path by which points move. The correct payoff is modest and powerful: some self-agreement must exist even before anyone knows where to look.
breaks_if: It breaks if the space is not the right closed filled shape, if the boundary has been removed, if the rule is not continuous, or if the rule sends points outside the domain. Each failure opens an escape route the theorem was designed to forbid.
everyday_test: Can the reader state the space, the rule, the inside-itself condition, the no-jump condition, and why the theorem proves existence rather than location? Make clear what would go wrong if the ball were open, hollow, or mapped outside itself.

name: Vector-field index
use_when: Use it when an arrow field has isolated defects and the question needs a signed local account of how arrows turn around each defect. The contract turns a nearby motion pattern into a number only after the defect has been separated from every other defect.
object_needed: The object is a vector field on a surface or state space, with one isolated defect enclosed by a small loop that contains no other defect. The loop is part of the evidence: it gives the reader a path for watching the surrounding arrows make one full turn account.
allowed_move: The allowed move is to clean or redraw the nearby arrow pattern while keeping the defect isolated and the surrounding loop meaningful for the same local failure. The redraw can simplify the arrows, but it cannot let another zero cross the loop or change which surface the arrows live on.
protected_evidence: The protected evidence is the signed turning of arrows during one trip around that one isolated defect, read from the surrounding loop before other defects enter. The index is therefore not a label placed on the defect; it is a record earned by walking around it and watching the arrows turn.
conclusion_it_can_force: It can turn a local failure of motion into countable evidence. It does not count how many equilibria exist, and it becomes global evidence only after all local indices are included. A single index says what this one defect contributes to the later whole-surface account.
breaks_if: It breaks if the defect is not isolated, if another defect lies inside the loop, if the arrows are not tangent to the claimed surface, or if the surface carrying the arrows has been modeled incorrectly. In those cases the loop is reading the wrong local event or more than one event at once.
everyday_test: Can the reader walk around the defect in words, say how the arrows turn during one full trip, and explain why no other defect is inside the loop? Also say why the count is local now and not yet the whole Poincare-Hopf total.

name: Poincare-Hopf theorem
use_when: Use it when every isolated vector-field defect on the right surface has been counted and the question concerns the total failure of the field. The theorem belongs only after the local index work is complete enough to be added across the entire carrier.
object_needed: The object is the entire surface carrying the vector field, plus the complete list of isolated defects and their indices on that same surface. The phrase 'same surface' does real work here: the local counts and the Euler characteristic must belong to one finished object.
allowed_move: The allowed move is to add all local indices and compare that total with the Euler characteristic of the same surface, without dropping boundary or defect data. Local cleanup is allowed only to make the defect list readable; it cannot change the surface account the total is being compared with.
protected_evidence: The protected evidence is the equality between the complete total local index and the Euler characteristic of that same surface, not one favorite defect. Poincare-Hopf is a whole-account statement: every local failure is entered into one ledger controlled by the carrier surface.
conclusion_it_can_force: It can force defects, forbid a nowhere-zero field on some surfaces, or show that local motion failures answer to whole-surface structure. It does not solve the differential equation, trace trajectories, or explain one equilibrium in isolation. Its conclusion is about the total account the field must pay.
breaks_if: It breaks if one defect is omitted, if the field is not on the claimed surface, if boundary behavior is ignored, if defects are not isolated, or if one equilibrium is treated as the whole theorem. Any missing entry turns a global statement into a partial inventory.
everyday_test: Can the reader name the surface, list every defect, add their signed indices, and say which Euler characteristic the total must match before claiming the theorem applies? Also state what the theorem does not provide: a path, a location recipe, or a full dynamics solution.

name: Configuration-space modeling
use_when: Use it when a physical or moving system is too hard to inspect directly and the question can be asked as a route, barrier, fixed-point, or defect problem. The modeling step is part of the proof; it decides what space the later theorem is actually allowed to see.
object_needed: The object is the space of all allowed states, with enough coordinates to describe one complete state and with forbidden states removed before the theorem is used. A point in this space must mean one real state of the system, not a convenient drawing that forgets a constraint.
allowed_move: The allowed move is to translate physical motion into paths through the state space without adding false freedoms, omitting real freedoms, or removing real barriers. A continuous path in the model is meaningful only if it represents a motion the real system could actually perform.
protected_evidence: The protected evidence is the shape of possible states: connected regions, holes, walls, fixed points, or total index constraints inside the honest model after forbidden states are removed. The theorem later reads this modeled shape, so the model's missing states and allowed paths carry the argument.
conclusion_it_can_force: It can show that a motion is blocked, that a special state must exist, or that a physical behavior is constrained before detailed equations are solved. It cannot rescue a dishonest model. The conclusion belongs to the physical system only if every modeled point and path has the promised real meaning.
breaks_if: It breaks if the state space forgets a real degree of freedom, includes forbidden collisions, or lets a theorem speak about a model that no longer represents the original system. It also breaks when a visual route in the model passes through a state the physical system could never occupy.
everyday_test: Can the reader describe one complete state, name the forbidden states, and explain how a path in the model represents real motion without passing through an impossible state? One useful check asks whether adding or removing one real constraint would change the shape the theorem sees.
